before.content_html:
Scalars and Vectors

Every physical quantity is either a scalar or a vector. Scalars have size only. Vectors have both size and direction. This distinction matters in physics: a car travelling at 20 m/s northwards and another travelling at 20 m/s southwards have the same speed but very different velocities.

Distance is a scalar — it measures the total length of path covered, with no regard for direction. Displacement is a vector — it measures how far an object is from its starting point in a straight line, and in which direction. A runner completing one lap of a 400 m track has covered 400 m distance but zero displacement.

Speed and Velocity

Speed is a scalar — it tells you how fast an object is moving but not the direction. The equation for speed is:

$$v = \frac{s}{t}$$

Where \(v\) is speed in m/s, \(s\) is distance in metres, and \(t\) is time in seconds. Rearranging gives \(s = vt\) and \(t = s / v\).

Key Fact

Typical speeds: walking ~1.5 m/s; running ~3 m/s; cycling ~6 m/s; car in a town ~13 m/s; car on a motorway ~30 m/s; sound in air ~330 m/s. These values are given as context — know the order of magnitude.

Velocity is a vector. It has both magnitude (speed) and direction. An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity because its direction changes continuously — this means it is accelerating even though its speed is constant.

Acceleration

Acceleration measures how quickly velocity changes. The equation is:

$$a = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

Where \(a\) is acceleration in m/s2, \(v\) is final velocity in m/s, \(u\) is initial velocity in m/s, and \(t\) is time in seconds. A negative value for \(a\) means the object is decelerating (slowing down).

Key Fact

For uniform (constant) acceleration when time is not given: \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\), where \(s\) is the distance covered. This equation is provided on the equation sheet — but you must be able to rearrange and apply it correctly.

A train accelerates uniformly from rest and travels 400 m before reaching 20 m/s. Calculate its acceleration.

Given: \(u = 0\) m/s, \(v = 20\) m/s, \(s = 400\) m. Using \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\):

\(20^2 = 0^2 + 2 \times a \times 400\)

\(400 = 800a\)

\(a = \frac{400}{800} = 0.5\) m/s2

Uniform vs Non-Uniform Acceleration

When an object experiences a constant resultant force, its acceleration is uniform — the same value throughout. A car on a straight motorway with constant engine force and negligible air resistance would have uniform acceleration. In contrast, real vehicles and falling objects experience non-uniform acceleration because resistive forces (air resistance, drag) increase with speed, gradually reducing the resultant force and therefore the acceleration.

On a velocity–time graph, uniform acceleration appears as a straight line (constant gradient). Non-uniform acceleration appears as a curve where the gradient decreases over time — such as the velocity of a sky diver before reaching terminal velocity, where the line levels off as drag builds up.

Distance–Time Graphs

A distance–time graph shows how far an object has moved from a reference point over time. The gradient (slope) of the line gives the speed.

  • A horizontal line means the object is stationary (gradient = 0, speed = 0).
  • A straight diagonal line means constant speed (constant gradient).
  • A curve getting steeper means increasing speed (acceleration). The instantaneous speed at any point on a curve is found by drawing a tangent at that point and calculating its gradient.

Velocity–Time Graphs

A velocity–time graph shows how velocity changes over time. Two key rules:

  • Gradient = acceleration. A steeply rising line means large acceleration; a falling line means deceleration.
  • Area under the graph = displacement (distance). Split the area into rectangles and triangles to calculate the total distance travelled.

A car accelerates from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s (triangle shape on the graph), then travels at 20 m/s for a further 20 s (rectangle). Calculate the total distance travelled.

Triangle area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m

Rectangle area = 20 × 20 = 400 m

Total distance = 100 + 400 = 500 m

Investigating Motion: Core Practical

A core practical for this topic involves investigating the relationship between acceleration and force or mass, often using a dynamics trolley and light gates on a measured track. Students measure the time for the trolley to pass through each light gate, calculate the change in velocity, and determine acceleration. By varying the applied force (using hanging masses on a pulley string) while keeping the trolley mass constant, the effect of force on acceleration can be plotted as a graph.

The key practical skills assessed include: correctly using light gates to measure velocity, identifying the independent variable (force or mass), controlling the dependent variable (acceleration), and recognising sources of error such as friction on the runway. Compensating for friction by tilting the runway slightly is a common technique — the trolley should move at constant speed without the hanging mass before adding a force.

A sprinter accelerates uniformly from rest to 9 m/s over a distance of 20 m during the first part of a race.

(b) State one assumption you made in your calculation. [1]

practice_questions.text:
A student records the motion of a toy car on a velocity–time graph. The car accelerates from 0 to 4 m/s over the first 5 seconds, travels at constant velocity for 10 seconds, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 4 seconds.
(a) Calculate the total distance travelled by the toy car. [3]
(b) Calculate the deceleration in the final 4 seconds. [2]
(c) On which section of the journey is the resultant force on the car zero? Explain why. [2]
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Triangle: ½ × 5 × 4 = 10 m [1]; Rectangle: 10 × 4 = 40 m [1]; Triangle: ½ × 4 × 4 = 8 m [1]; Total = 58 m [accept if ECF consistent]
(b) a = (0 − 4) / 4 = −1 m/s² [1]; deceleration = 1 m/s² [1]

before.content_html:
Resultant Forces and Newton’s First Law

A resultant force is the overall force on an object once all individual forces are combined. Forces are vectors, so direction matters: two forces of 10 N in opposite directions give a resultant of zero; two forces of 10 N in the same direction give a resultant of 20 N.

Newton’s first law (Sir Isaac Newton, 1643–1727, published in Principia Mathematica, 1687) states that an object will remain at rest or continue to move at a constant velocity unless a non-zero resultant force acts on it. In other words: no resultant force means no change in motion. This is also why inertia — an object’s resistance to change in motion — increases with mass.

Key Fact

Newton’s first law: a resultant force of zero means no change in motion. An object at rest stays at rest; a moving object keeps moving at constant velocity. Inertia resists changes — heavier objects have more inertia and are harder to accelerate or stop.

Newton’s Second Law and F = ma

Newton’s second law states that the resultant force on an object is directly proportional to its acceleration and inversely proportional to its mass:

$$F = m a$$

Where \(F\) is resultant force in newtons (N), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(a\) is acceleration in m/s2. Rearranging: \(a = F/m\) and \(m = F/a\).

In this core practical, a trolley on a smooth runway is accelerated by hanging masses on a string over a pulley. Light gates measure the time for the trolley to pass through, allowing calculation of velocity and acceleration. The independent variable is the force applied (changed by moving masses from the trolley to the hanger, keeping total mass constant); the dependent variable is acceleration; controlled variables include total system mass, surface friction, and runway angle.

Plotting force (y-axis) against acceleration (x-axis) gives a straight line through the origin, confirming \(F \propto a\). The gradient equals the mass of the trolley. Keeping total mass constant is essential — if you add mass to the hanger without removing it from the trolley, both force and mass change, so results are meaningless.

A 1500 kg car has a driving force of 6000 N. Friction and air resistance total 1500 N. Calculate the acceleration.

Step 1: Resultant force = 6000 − 1500 = 4500 N

Step 2: \(a = F / m = 4500 / 1500 = 3\) m/s2

Newton’s Third Law

Newton’s third law states that for every force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force. The key points: the two forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, act on different objects, and are the same type of force. A swimmer pushes water backwards (action); the water pushes the swimmer forwards (reaction).

Students often confuse Newton’s third law with balanced forces. Balanced forces act on the same object (e.g. weight and normal reaction on a resting book). Newton’s third law pairs always act on different objects: the book pushes down on the table (gravity transmitted), the table pushes up on the book.

Weight and Terminal Velocity

The weight of an object is the gravitational force on it:

$$W = m g$$

Where \(W\) is weight in newtons, \(m\) is mass in kg, and \(g\) is gravitational field strength (10 N/kg near Earth’s surface). Mass is the amount of matter in an object (kg); weight changes with gravitational field strength; mass does not.

When an object falls through a fluid (air or liquid), drag increases as speed increases. Eventually drag equals weight and the resultant force is zero — the object reaches terminal velocity. A skydiver opening a parachute dramatically increases drag, decelerating to a lower terminal velocity (suitable for landing).

Key Fact

At terminal velocity: weight = drag, resultant force = 0, velocity is constant. Before terminal velocity: weight > drag, resultant force downward, object accelerates. When parachute opens: drag > weight, resultant force upward, object decelerates to a new lower terminal velocity.

Stopping Distance

The total stopping distance of a vehicle has two components. Thinking distance is the distance covered while the driver reacts; it increases with speed and is worsened by tiredness, alcohol, drugs, or distraction. Braking distance is the distance covered while the brakes slow the vehicle; it increases with speed, wet/icy roads, worn tyres, and worn brakes.

Total stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. At higher speeds, braking distance increases much more than linearly (because kinetic energy is proportional to \(v^2\)), so doubling speed more than doubles braking distance.

Momentum and Its Conservation

Momentum (\(p\)) is calculated as:

$$p = m v$$

Where \(p\) is momentum in kg m/s, \(m\) is mass in kg, and \(v\) is velocity in m/s. Momentum is a vector — direction matters.

The law of conservation of momentum states that in a closed system (no external forces), total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after. This principle underpins how engineers design car crumple zones, safety barriers, and space probes.

A 1000 kg car moving at 12 m/s collides with and joins to a stationary 500 kg car. Calculate their combined velocity after the collision.

Momentum before = \(1000 \times 12 + 500 \times 0 = 12\,000\) kg m/s

Momentum after = \((1000 + 500) \times v = 1500v\)

Conservation: \(1500v = 12\,000\)

\(v = 12\,000 / 1500 = 8\) m/s

B) Every action has an equal and opposite reaction

practice_questions.marks: Speed increases (accelerates) initially [1]; as speed increases, drag increases [1]; when drag equals weight, resultant force is zero and terminal velocity is reached (constant speed) [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why braking distance increases much more than thinking distance when a driver doubles their speed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear quantitative reasoning linking kinetic energy or stopping distance to speed squared.
Secure: Both distances addressed with causal explanation.
Developing: One distance explained; limited comparison.
Emerging: Simple relevant point.

Credit points:

• Doubling speed doubles thinking distance [1]

practice_questions.text:
A 800 kg trolley moving at 6 m/s east collides with a stationary 400 kg crate. After the collision, the crate moves east at 8 m/s.
(a) Calculate the total momentum before the collision. [2]
(b) Calculate the velocity of the trolley after the collision. State the direction of motion. [2]
practice_questions.marks:
(a) p = mv = 800 × 6 = 4800 kg m/s (east) [1]; crate p = 0; total = 4800 kg m/s [1]
(b) Momentum after: crate = 400 × 8 = 3200 kg m/s; trolley momentum after = 4800 − 3200 = 1600 kg m/s [1]; v = 1600 / 800 = 2 m/s east [1].

practice_questions.text: A student investigates Newton's second law using a trolley, pulley, and hanging masses on a runway. Describe how the student should set up and carry out the investigation, including what measurements to take, how to ensure a fair test, and how to use the results to confirm Newton's second law.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Systematic method with IV, DV, controls, repeats, and analysis plan clearly linked to F = ma.
Secure: IV, DV, and controls identified; method mostly complete.
Developing: Some steps described but missing key controls or analysis.
Emerging: Simple relevant points.

Credit points (any 6):
• Attach string from trolley over pulley to hanging masses [1]
• Use light gates (or ticker timer) to measure time and calculate acceleration [1]
• Independent variable: force (number of masses on hanger) [1]
• Dependent variable: acceleration [1]
• Control: keep total mass of system constant (move masses from trolley to hanger, not add) [1]
• Carry out repeats and calculate mean acceleration for each force [1]
• Plot graph of F (y-axis) against a (x-axis) [1]
• Straight line through origin confirms F ∝ a, confirming Newton's second law [1]

lessons.title: Conservation of Energy, Stores and Transfers

before.content_html:
Energy Stores

Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred between energy stores. The key stores to know are: kinetic, thermal (heat), chemical, elastic potential, gravitational potential (GPE), electrostatic, magnetic, and nuclear. Each store holds energy until a transfer pathway moves it elsewhere.

Kinetic energy is the energy stored in a moving object. It is calculated using:

$$E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$$

Where \(E_k\) is kinetic energy in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(v\) is speed in m/s. Notice that doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy (because of \(v^2\)).

Key Fact

Eight energy stores: kinetic, thermal, chemical, elastic potential, gravitational potential, electrostatic, magnetic, nuclear. Key equation: \(E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\). Doubling speed quadruples \(E_k\); doubling mass only doubles it. This explains why faster vehicles are much harder to stop.

Gravitational Potential Energy

Gravitational potential energy (GPE) is calculated using:

$$E_p = m g h$$

Where \(E_p\) is GPE in joules, \(m\) is mass in kg, \(g\) is gravitational field strength (10 N/kg near Earth’s surface), and \(h\) is height in metres. GPE increases when an object is raised and decreases when it falls.

Elastic potential energy is stored in stretched or compressed elastic objects (springs, rubber bands):

$$E_e = \frac{1}{2} k e^2$$

Where \(E_e\) is elastic potential energy in J, \(k\) is the spring constant in N/m, and \(e\) is the extension (or compression) in metres. This equation only applies below the limit of proportionality — beyond this, the spring deforms permanently and the equation no longer holds.

Energy Transfer Pathways

Energy moves between stores via four transfer pathways: by mechanical work (a force moving an object), by electrical work (a current doing work), by heating (thermal conduction, convection, or radiation), and by radiation (electromagnetic or sound waves). The pathway is not the same as the store — heating is a pathway; thermal energy is a store.

A useful example: when a ball is thrown upwards, energy transfers from the kinetic store (moving ball) to the gravitational potential store (raised ball). At the peak, the ball is momentarily still — kinetic store is empty, GPE store is at its maximum. As the ball falls, the transfer reverses.

A 3 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Assuming all GPE converts to kinetic energy (no air resistance), calculate the speed just before it hits the ground.

Step 1: \(E_p = mgh = 3 \times 10 \times 5 = 150\) J

Step 2: Set \(E_k = E_p\): \(\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = 150\)

Step 3: \(v^2 = \frac{2 \times 150}{3} = 100\); so \(v = 10\) m/s

The Law of Conservation of Energy

The law of conservation of energy states that the total energy in a closed system always remains constant. Energy is never lost — it is transferred usefully, or it is dissipated (spread out to the thermal store of the surroundings). In a real system, some energy is always dissipated as thermal energy.

Key Fact

Conservation of energy: total energy in a closed system is constant. In a real motor, input electrical energy = useful kinetic energy output + thermal energy dissipated. Energy is not ‘lost’ — it is spread out as low-grade heat in the surroundings.

Mechanical Work Done

When a force moves an object through a distance, energy is transferred as mechanical work:

$$W = F s$$

Where \(W\) is work done in joules, \(F\) is force in newtons, and \(s\) is the distance moved along the direction of the force in metres. 1 joule = 1 newton–metre. If you push a wall and it doesn’t move, no work is done — even if you exert a large force.

Efficiency

Efficiency measures how well a device converts input energy to useful output energy:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy}}{\text{total input energy}}$$

Efficiency can be expressed as a decimal (e.g. 0.75) or a percentage (75%). No real device is 100% efficient because some energy is always dissipated as thermal energy. Efficiency can also be calculated using power: efficiency = useful output power / total input power.

An electric motor receives 600 J of electrical energy and transfers 450 J as useful kinetic energy. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage.

Efficiency = 450 / 600 = 0.75 = 75%

The remaining 150 J (25%) is dissipated as thermal energy in the motor’s windings. Efficiency could be improved by reducing friction in the bearings or using better insulating materials.

Power

Power is the rate of energy transfer or the rate of doing work:

490647P = \frac{E}{t} = \frac{W}{t}490647

Where \(P\) is power in watts (W), \(E\) is energy in joules, \(W\) is work done in joules, and \(t\) is time in seconds. One watt equals one joule per second. A 100 W light bulb transfers 100 J of energy every second. For a force moving an object at constant speed, power can also be written as \(P = Fv\), where \(v\) is speed in m/s — useful when calculating engine power output.

The specific heat capacity practical investigates how much energy is needed to raise the temperature of a substance by 1 °C per kg. A metal block is heated electrically using a known power supply; temperature is measured at regular time intervals. The energy supplied is calculated as \(E = P \times t\), and specific heat capacity is found from \(Q = mc\Delta T\) rearranged to \(c = Q / (m \Delta T)\). Insulating the block and using a thermometer in the centre of the block reduce systematic errors from heat loss and uneven temperature distribution.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a non-renewable energy resource?
A) Solar
B) Tidal
C) Natural gas
D) Geothermal
practice_questions.marks: C) Natural gas [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one environmental advantage and one environmental disadvantage of using wind turbines to generate electricity.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage: no carbon dioxide (or greenhouse gas) emissions during operation [1 mark]. Disadvantage: any one of — noise for nearby residents; visual impact on landscape; variable output dependent on wind speed; habitat disruption during construction [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A tidal barrage generates 4,500,000 J of energy in 900 s. Calculate the power output of the barrage. Give your answer in kilowatts.
practice_questions.marks: P = E/t [1 mark]; P = 4,500,000 ÷ 900 = 5,000 W [1 mark]; = 5 kW [1 mark — with correct unit].

practice_questions.text: Explain why fossil fuels are described as non-renewable, and explain two environmental problems caused by burning them.
practice_questions.marks: Non-renewable: formed over millions of years so cannot be replaced within a human timescale — once used, the supply is permanently reduced [1 mark]. Problem 1: burning releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the atmosphere and contributes to global warming / climate change [1 mark + development for link to consequence, 1 mark]. Problem 2: burning coal/oil releases sulfur dioxide which dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain, damaging ecosystems and buildings [1 mark]. (Any two well-explained problems: 2 marks.)

practice_questions.text: A household uses a 3 kW electric shower for 8 minutes every day. Calculate the total energy transferred by the shower in one week (7 days). Give your answer in joules.
practice_questions.marks: Step 1: Convert power to watts — 3 kW = 3,000 W [1 mark]. Step 2: Convert time to seconds per day — 8 × 60 = 480 s [1 mark]. Step 3: Energy per day — E = Pt = 3,000 × 480 = 1,440,000 J [1 mark]. Step 4: Total for one week — 1,440,000 × 7 = 10,080,000 J [1 mark + unit mark: J]. Mastering: all steps correct with clear working, correct unit [5–6]. Secure: minor arithmetic slip but correct method [3–4]. Developing: power or time conversion correct but one major error [2]. Emerging: formula stated but substitution incorrect [1].

practice_questions.text: 'Renewable energy sources will always be preferable to fossil fuels for generating electricity.' Evaluate this statement, referring to specific energy resources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments supporting the statement: renewables produce no CO2 during operation, reducing climate change; they will not run out unlike finite fossil fuels; solar and wind have decreasing costs; tidal is highly predictable. Arguments against: many renewables are weather-dependent (solar/wind produce nothing on calm, cloudy days); fossil fuels are reliable and can respond to peak demand instantly; renewables often require large land areas or coastal locations; biofuels still release CO2 when burned. Evaluative conclusion: neither type is universally preferable — the best choice depends on location, reliability requirements and available storage infrastructure. A balanced national energy mix is typically more practical than 100% renewables without large-scale storage. Mastering: sustained, well-organised argument with named resources, specific impacts, and a justified conclusion reaching beyond 'it depends'. Secure: clear points on both sides with developed examples. Developing: relevant points but limited analysis. Emerging: simple points, little evaluation.

lessons.title: Waves: Properties, Wave Equation and Behaviour

before.content_html:
What Are Waves?

Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter. The particles of the medium oscillate about their rest positions — they do not travel with the wave. Evidence for this can be seen with water waves: a floating object bobs up and down but does not travel along with the wave front.

There are two fundamental types. In a transverse wave, the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. All electromagnetic waves and water waves are transverse. In a longitudinal wave, the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Sound and P-waves (primary seismic waves) are longitudinal.

Longitudinal waves create alternating regions of compression (particles squeezed close) and rarefaction (particles spread out). You can model this with a Slinky spring: push it lengthways to see compressions and rarefactions travel along it.

Key Fact

Transverse waves: oscillations perpendicular to direction of travel (e.g. light, water waves). Longitudinal waves: oscillations parallel to direction of travel (e.g. sound, P-waves). All waves transfer energy without transferring matter.

Wave Properties

Every wave can be described using four properties:

Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position. A larger amplitude means the wave carries more energy.

Wavelength (symbol \(\lambda\)) is the distance from one point on a wave to the identical point on the next wave, e.g. crest to crest.

Frequency (symbol \(f\)) is the number of complete waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz (Hz).

The period (symbol \(T\)) is the time for one complete wave and is linked to frequency by: $$T = \frac{1}{f}$$ If \(f = 50\) Hz, then \(T = \frac{1}{50} = 0.02\) s.

The Wave Equation

Wave speed, frequency and wavelength are related by two equivalent forms of the wave equation that you must be able to recall and apply:

$$v = f \lambda$$

$$v = \frac{x}{t}$$

Where \(v\) is wave speed in metres per second (m/s), \(f\) is frequency in hertz (Hz), \(\lambda\) is wavelength in metres (m), \(x\) is distance in metres and \(t\) is time in seconds.

Key Fact

Both wave equations must be recalled: \(v = f\lambda\) (speed = frequency × wavelength) and \(v = x/t\) (speed = distance ÷ time). Common rearrangement: \(f = v / \lambda\) and \(\lambda = v / f\).

Example 1: A sound wave has a frequency of 440 Hz and a wavelength of 0.75 m. Calculate the wave speed.

\(v = f\lambda = 440 \times 0.75 = 330\) m/s

Example 2: A water wave travels 12 m in 4 s. Calculate the wave speed, then find the wavelength if the frequency is 1.5 Hz.

Speed: \(v = x/t = 12/4 = 3\) m/s. Wavelength: \(\lambda = v/f = 3/1.5 = 2\) m.

Always check: speed in m/s, frequency in Hz, wavelength in m. Do not mix units.

Reflection and Refraction

When waves reach a boundary between two different materials, they may be reflected, refracted, transmitted or absorbed — often a mixture of all four.

Reflection occurs when a wave bounces off a surface. The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (a line perpendicular to the surface at the point of contact).

Refraction occurs when a wave changes speed as it crosses a boundary. If the wave slows down, it bends towards the normal; if it speeds up, it bends away. Frequency does not change during refraction — only speed and wavelength change.

Key Fact

During refraction: speed changes, wavelength changes, frequency stays the same. Direction changes if the wave crosses the boundary at an angle (no direction change if it arrives along the normal).

Core Practical: Wave Speed in a Solid and a Fluid

The core practical requires you to investigate the suitability of equipment to measure wave speed, frequency and wavelength in both a solid and a fluid.

Fluid (ripple tank): A vibrating bar or dipper creates water waves on the surface. A stroboscope can be used to ‘freeze’ the wave pattern. Measure the wavelength directly from the wave pattern projected onto a screen. Measure frequency using the stroboscope setting or a timer. Calculate speed using \(v = f\lambda\). Alternatively, time how long it takes waves to travel a measured distance: \(v = x/t\).

Solid (metal rod): Strike one end of a metal rod with a hammer; the vibration travels as a compression wave along the rod. A microphone at the far end detects when the pulse arrives. With two microphones at a known separation, a data logger records the time between signals. Calculate speed from \(v = x/t\). Evaluate suitability: the rod method is more precise because water waves are affected by surface tension and depth variations.

Seismic Waves, Ultrasound and Infrasound

Sound is only audible to humans between about 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz. Ultrasound (above 20,000 Hz) has uses in foetal scanning, sonar depth-finding and industrial flaw detection. Infrasound (below 20 Hz) is used to study seismic activity and can travel vast distances.

Seismic P-waves (longitudinal) travel through both solids and liquids. S-waves (transverse) can only travel through solids. The detection of S-waves and P-waves by seismographs provides evidence for the internal structure of the Earth.

before.content_html:
The Electromagnetic Spectrum

The electromagnetic (EM) spectrum is a continuous family of transverse waves. All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum — the speed of light, \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s — and can travel through empty space without needing a medium. All EM waves are transverse: their oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel.

The seven main groupings in order of decreasing wavelength (and increasing frequency) are:

radio waves → microwaves → infrared → visible light → ultraviolet → X-rays → gamma rays.

A useful mnemonic: Red Monkeys In Vests Usually Xcel Gloriously. Because all EM waves travel at the same speed, waves with higher frequency must have shorter wavelength (from \(v = f\lambda\) with constant \(v\)).

Key Fact

All seven EM wave types are transverse, travel at \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum, transfer energy from source to observer, and obey \(v = f\lambda\). Order (decreasing wavelength): radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

Uses and Dangers of EM Waves

Each region of the spectrum has properties that make it suited to specific applications, but higher-frequency waves are generally more dangerous because they carry more energy and are more ionising.

Radio waves are used for broadcasting (TV and radio), satellite transmission and long-distance communication. They can diffract around hills and buildings. Radio waves can be produced by oscillating electrical circuits and can also induce oscillations in aerial circuits when they are received.

Microwaves are used in satellite communication, mobile phone networks and cooking. In microwave ovens, the waves are absorbed by water molecules, causing them to vibrate and heat the food. Danger: internal heating of body cells — avoid prolonged direct exposure.

Infrared (IR) radiation is emitted by all warm objects. Uses include thermal imaging cameras, television remote controls, short-range optical fibre communications, cooking (grills, toasters) and security systems. Danger: skin burns from excessive exposure.

Visible light is the narrow band our eyes detect, from red (longest wavelength in this range) to violet (shortest). Uses: photography, illumination, optical fibre communication. The different colours of visible light correspond to different frequencies.

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation causes skin to tan and can damage surface cells, leading to sunburn and increasing the risk of skin cancer. UV is used in fluorescent lamps, security marking and detecting forged banknotes (which do not fluoresce like genuine notes). Danger: damage to surface cells and eyes.

X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by denser materials such as bone and metal. Uses: medical imaging (radiographs), airport security scanners, detecting internal flaws in metal structures. Danger: cell damage and increased mutation risk — medical staff use lead shielding and minimise exposure time.

Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and highest frequency. They are emitted by radioactive nuclei and are highly penetrating. Uses: radiotherapy (killing cancer tumours), sterilising food and medical equipment, and as tracers in medical imaging. Danger: mutation or damage to cells in the body — lead or thick concrete shielding required.

Key Fact

Danger increases with frequency: radio and microwaves pose low risk at typical exposure levels; UV damages surface cells and eyes; X-rays and gamma rays can cause cell mutation, damage to DNA and cancer. Higher frequency = more energy per photon = greater ionising effect.

Refraction and Ray Diagrams

When light crosses a boundary between materials of different optical densities, it refracts (changes direction). The ray is described relative to the normal — a line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.

The angle of incidence is measured between the incoming ray and the normal. The angle of refraction is measured between the refracted ray and the normal. When light enters a denser medium (e.g. air into glass), it slows down and bends towards the normal. When it exits into a less dense medium, it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

Place a rectangular glass block on plain paper. Shine a narrow ray of light at the flat face at an angle. Draw around the block and mark where the ray enters and exits. Remove the block and use a ruler to draw the complete ray path, including the refracted ray inside the glass. Measure the angle of incidence and angle of refraction at both surfaces using a protractor. Record how the ray bends towards the normal on entering the glass and away from the normal on leaving.

This experiment demonstrates: (a) refraction changes direction at a boundary; (b) the ray inside the glass travels in a straight line; (c) the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but displaced sideways. Control variables include: distance of the light source, use of the same glass block throughout.

Snell’s law gives the quantitative relationship between the angles of incidence and refraction: \(n_1 \sin \theta_1 = n_2 \sin \theta_2\), where \(n\) is the refractive index of each medium and \(\theta\) is the angle measured from the normal. For light travelling from air (\(n \approx 1\)) into glass (\(n \approx 1.5\)), the refracted ray is bent towards the normal.

Infrared Emission and Absorption

All bodies emit infrared radiation. The hotter an object, the more infrared it emits and the shorter its peak emission wavelength. For a body to remain at a constant temperature, the average power it radiates must equal the average power it absorbs. If it absorbs more than it emits, it warms up; if it radiates more than it absorbs, it cools down.

The intensity and wavelength distribution of radiation emitted by a body depend on its surface temperature. This principle underpins our understanding of how the Earth’s temperature is regulated: the planet absorbs solar radiation and re-emits infrared. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb some of this outgoing infrared and re-emit it in all directions, reducing net heat loss — the greenhouse effect.

Fill a Leslie cube (a hollow metal cube with four different surface finishes: matt black, shiny black, matt white, shiny white) with hot water. Place an infrared detector at an equal distance from each face in turn and record the radiation emitted. Result: matt black emits the most infrared; shiny silver (or white) emits the least. This confirms that dark, matt surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers of infrared, while shiny surfaces are the poorest emitters (best reflectors).

glossary_terms.definition: The continuous range of electromagnetic waves, ordered by wavelength or frequency, from radio waves to gamma rays. All travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
Electromagnetic waves with the longest wavelengths in the spectrum, used for broadcasting, satellite communications and long-distance signalling.
Electromagnetic waves between radio and infrared; used in satellite communication, mobile phones and microwave ovens.
Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths just longer than red visible light; emitted by all warm objects and used in remote controls, thermal imaging and optical fibres.
Electromagnetic radiation with frequencies just above violet visible light; causes tanning and fluorescence, used in security marking and detecting forged banknotes.
High-energy electromagnetic waves that pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone; used in medical imaging and airport security scanners.
The highest-frequency electromagnetic waves, emitted by radioactive nuclei; used in cancer treatment, sterilisation and medical tracers.
An imaginary line drawn perpendicular to a surface at the point where a ray meets it; used as the reference line for measuring angles of incidence and refraction.
The angle between an incident ray and the normal at the point of incidence.
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal at the point of refraction.
A law relating the angles of incidence and refraction at a boundary between two media: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, where n is the refractive index of each medium.

before.exam_tip_html: For EM spectrum questions, learn the order of waves and one use and one danger for each type — these appear in both multiple choice and extended-response questions. When drawing ray diagrams for refraction, always draw the normal first as a dashed line, then measure angles from it, not from the surface. A common error is measuring the angle of incidence from the surface instead of the normal, giving the complement of the correct angle. For higher-tier Snell’s law questions, always quote the formula, substitute in the known values, and give your answer to 2–3 significant figures with the correct unit (refractive index has no unit).

Secure (5–7): covers emission–absorption balance and greenhouse effect with some development. Developing (3–4): relevant points on emission and temperature but limited explanation of Earth's balance. Emerging (1–2): states that hotter objects emit more radiation.

before.content_html:
How the Atomic Model Has Developed

Our understanding of atomic structure has been revised several times as new experimental evidence emerged. The earliest scientific model, proposed by Dalton in the early 1800s, described atoms as tiny, indivisible solid spheres — a solid sphere model that could not explain electrical phenomena.

In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model. The atom was described as a ball of positive charge with negative electrons scattered throughout it. This model was overturned by Ernest Rutherford’s gold foil experiment.

Key Fact

In 1909, Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through (atom is mostly empty space); some deflected at large angles; a very few bounced straight back (dense positive nucleus exists). This led to the nuclear model of the atom.

Niels Bohr (1913) refined the nuclear model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus only in specific, fixed energy levels or shells. This explained why atoms emit and absorb specific frequencies of electromagnetic radiation. James Chadwick completed the picture in 1932 by discovering the neutron, confirming that nuclei contain both protons and neutrons.

The structure of an atom is described using two numbers in the standard notation \(^A_Z\text{X}\): the mass (nucleon) number \(A\) gives the total number of protons plus neutrons; the atomic (proton) number \(Z\) gives the number of protons. Electrons orbit the nucleus at set distances, and atoms are electrically neutral because the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

Radioactive Decay

Some nuclei are unstable and emit radiation to become more stable. This is radioactive decay. It is a random process — it is impossible to predict when a specific nucleus will decay, but for a large sample of nuclei the statistical behaviour is predictable.

Radioactive decay can be detected using a Geiger-Müller tube (GM tube) or photographic film. Any measurement of radioactivity must subtract background radiation — the low-level ionising radiation always present from natural and artificial sources.

Key Fact

Three types of ionising radiation are emitted from unstable nuclei: alpha (\(\alpha\)), beta-minus (\(\beta^-\)), beta-plus (\(\beta^+\)) and gamma (\(\gamma\)). Also, neutron emission is possible. All four are ionising. Alpha is most ionising but least penetrating; gamma is least ionising but most penetrating.

Alpha, Beta and Gamma Radiation

Alpha (\(\alpha\)) particle: two protons and two neutrons — equivalent to a helium-4 nucleus (\(^4_2\text{He}\)). Alpha particles are strongly ionising but have very low penetrating power: they are stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper. In alpha decay, the parent nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons: mass number decreases by 4, proton number decreases by 2.

Beta-minus (\(\beta^-\)) decay: a neutron transforms into a proton, emitting a high-speed electron. The proton number increases by 1; the mass number stays the same. Stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Moderately ionising.

Beta-plus (\(\beta^+\)) / positron emission: a proton transforms into a neutron, emitting a positron (the antimatter equivalent of an electron). The proton number decreases by 1; the mass number stays the same. Used in PET scanning (positron emission tomography).

Gamma (\(\gamma\)) radiation: high-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus after alpha or beta decay, as the nucleus loses excess energy. No change to proton or mass number. Only significantly reduced by several centimetres of lead or thick concrete. Weakly ionising but highly penetrating.

Balanced Nuclear Equations

In a nuclear equation, both the total mass number and the total proton number must be conserved (balanced) on both sides of the arrow. The general rule: \(\sum A\) and \(\sum Z\) are each equal before and after the decay.

Alpha decay of radium-226:

$$^{226}_{88}\text{Ra} \rightarrow ^{222}_{86}\text{Rn} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$$

Check: top (226 = 222 + 4 ✓); bottom (88 = 86 + 2 ✓).

Beta-minus decay of carbon-14:

$$^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + ^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$$

Check: top (14 = 14 + 0 ✓); bottom (6 = 7 + (−1) ✓).

Beta-plus decay: proton number decreases by 1, mass number unchanged, positron emitted (\(^0_{+1}\text{e}\)).

Key Fact

In any nuclear equation: mass numbers (top) must balance on both sides; proton numbers (bottom) must balance on both sides. Alpha: −4 mass, −2 proton. Beta-minus: 0 mass, +1 proton. Beta-plus: 0 mass, −1 proton. Gamma: no change to either number.

Half-Life

The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for half the undecayed nuclei to decay, or for the activity to fall to half its original value. Because decay is random, it cannot be predicted when a specific nucleus will decay — but half-life allows us to predict the statistical behaviour of a very large number of nuclei.

After one half-life: \(\frac{1}{2}\) of the original nuclei remain. After two half-lives: \(\frac{1}{4}\) remain. After three half-lives: \(\frac{1}{8}\) remain. The activity decreases by the same ratio each half-life.

A radioactive sample has an activity of 1,600 Bq. After 40 minutes the activity is 200 Bq. Calculate the half-life.

Number of halvings: \(1600 \rightarrow 800 \rightarrow 400 \rightarrow 200\) = three half-lives.

Three half-lives = 40 minutes, so one half-life = \(40 \div 3 \approx 13.3\) minutes.

Common error: do not confuse ‘fraction remaining’ with ‘fraction decayed’. After 3 half-lives, \(\frac{1}{8}\) remains and \(\frac{7}{8}\) has decayed.

Background Radiation

Background radiation comes from natural sources (radon gas from the ground, cosmic rays, food and drink containing trace radioactive isotopes, building materials) and artificial sources (medical procedures such as X-rays, emissions from the nuclear industry). It must always be subtracted from measured count rates to obtain the count rate from a source alone.

lessons.title: Uses and Dangers of Radiation, Fission and Fusion

before.content_html:
Uses of Radioactivity

Ionising radiation, though hazardous, has well-established uses in medicine, food safety and industry. Each application exploits a specific property of a particular radiation type.

Household smoke alarms use a small americium-241 source emitting alpha particles. Alpha particles ionise air between two electrodes, maintaining a small current. Smoke particles absorb the alpha particles, reducing the current and triggering the alarm. Alpha is chosen because it is strongly ionising (effective at ionising air) and does not penetrate the housing, so it poses minimal risk outside the device.

Irradiating food: gamma rays from a radioactive source are used to kill bacteria and other pathogens in food, extending shelf life without significantly affecting taste or nutrition. The food itself does not become radioactive.

Sterilisation of medical equipment uses gamma rays to kill micro-organisms on surgical instruments. This is preferred for heat-sensitive items that cannot withstand autoclaving.

Thickness gauging: beta sources are used in manufacturing to control the thickness of paper, metal sheet or plastic film. Beta radiation partially penetrates the material; a detector on the other side monitors the intensity. If the material is too thick, less radiation reaches the detector; the machinery adjusts accordingly. Beta is used (not alpha, which would be blocked entirely, or gamma, which would pass through without being affected by small thickness changes).

Tracing: radioactive tracers are injected or ingested and their progress through a system monitored externally. In medicine, tracers help diagnose blockages in blood vessels or thyroid disorders. In industry, tracers locate leaks in underground pipes.

Diagnosis and Treatment of Cancer

Gamma radiation is used in radiotherapy to destroy tumour cells. An external beam is targeted at the tumour from multiple angles to maximise the dose at the tumour while minimising damage to surrounding healthy tissue. For internal tumours, radioactive implants (seeds) can be placed directly inside or near the tumour.

A PET scanner uses a tracer that emits positrons (beta-plus particles). The positron immediately annihilates with a nearby electron, producing two gamma rays that travel in exactly opposite directions. Detectors surrounding the patient record these paired gamma rays and reconstruct a 3D image of metabolic activity, helping identify tumours and brain conditions.

The tracer used in PET scanners must have a short half-life to limit the patient’s radiation dose, and must also decay by positron emission. Fluorine-18 is widely used, with a half-life of approximately 110 minutes. Because of this short half-life, the tracer must be produced in a nearby cyclotron and used quickly — it cannot be transported over long distances or stored for later use.

Contamination vs Irradiation

It is essential to distinguish between two types of radiation hazard:

Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an outside source. The exposed object or person does not become radioactive. Irradiation from a gamma source (e.g. during a medical scan) stops as soon as the source is moved away.

Contamination occurs when radioactive material gets onto or inside the body. This is potentially more dangerous because the radioactive source remains close to cells and continues to irradiate them. Alpha contamination is particularly dangerous: outside the body, alpha is stopped by skin, but if inhaled or ingested, alpha particles are absorbed by internal organs at very short range.

Key Fact

Irradiation: external, exposure stops when source moves. Contamination: internal (on or in the body), continuous exposure, harder to control. Alpha contamination is especially dangerous inside the body despite low external penetrating power.

Safety Precautions

Precautions to reduce radiation dose include: keeping radioactive sources in lead-lined containers, using tongs or remote handling to avoid direct contact, minimising the time spent near sources, maintaining maximum possible distance from sources, wearing dosimetry badges to monitor cumulative dose, and ensuring patients receive the minimum dose necessary for diagnosis or treatment.

Nuclear Fission

Nuclear fission occurs when a large, unstable nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller daughter nuclei, releasing two or three more neutrons and a large amount of energy. The most commonly used fissile material is uranium-235 (U-235).

Each fission event releases neutrons that can trigger further fissions in neighbouring U-235 nuclei. If each event causes on average more than one further fission, a chain reaction develops. In an uncontrolled chain reaction, energy release escalates exponentially (as in a nuclear weapon). In a nuclear reactor, the chain reaction is kept controlled so that on average exactly one new fission is triggered per event.

Control is achieved using: control rods (made of boron or hafnium) that absorb excess neutrons — inserting them deeper into the reactor slows or stops the chain reaction; a moderator (commonly graphite or water) that slows the neutrons down to a speed at which they are most effective at causing fission. The thermal energy released is used to heat water, producing steam to drive turbines that generate electricity. The products of fission (daughter nuclei) are radioactive and must be stored safely.

Key Fact

Moderator: slows neutrons to a speed where they are effective at causing fission. Control rods: absorb neutrons to regulate the rate of the chain reaction. Inserting rods further slows or stops the reaction; withdrawing them speeds it up.

Nuclear Fusion

Nuclear fusion is the process by which two light nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus. The total mass after fusion is slightly less than the total mass before; this ‘missing’ mass is released as energy. Fusion releases much more energy per kilogram of fuel than fission and its reactants (such as deuterium and tritium, both isotopes of hydrogen) are relatively abundant.

Fusion is the energy source of stars, including our Sun. In stellar cores, extreme gravitational pressure and temperatures many millions of degrees Celsius provide the conditions for sustained fusion. On Earth, reproducing these conditions is enormously challenging: the positively charged nuclei repel each other strongly (electrostatic repulsion), so they must be given enough kinetic energy to overcome this barrier, requiring temperatures of tens of millions of degrees.

At the extreme temperatures needed for fusion, matter exists as a plasma — electrons are stripped from atoms, leaving a gas of free nuclei and electrons. This plasma cannot be contained by physical materials (it would instantly vaporise any wall) and must be held in place by powerful magnetic fields (as in a tokamak design) or compressed by powerful lasers.

The main engineering challenges are: reaching and sustaining the required temperature (tens of millions of kelvin); confining the plasma without it touching the reactor walls; and achieving net energy gain (the energy output from fusion exceeds the energy input to heat and confine the plasma). International research projects are working towards making fusion a practical, economic energy source, but as of the mid-2020s no fusion reactor has yet achieved sustained net energy gain at a power-plant scale.

Key Fact

Fission: large nucleus splits, releases neutrons and energy, fuel = U-235. Fusion: light nuclei combine, loss of mass releases energy, fuel = hydrogen isotopes (deuterium, tritium). Fusion powers stars. Both are sources of nuclear energy; neither involves combustion.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly explains why alpha sources are used in household smoke alarms?
A) Alpha particles penetrate through the housing to detect smoke outside
B) Alpha particles ionise the air between electrodes; smoke absorbs them, reducing the current
C) Alpha particles are reflected by smoke particles, triggering the alarm
D) Alpha particles are weakly ionising, making them safe for household use
practice_questions.marks: B) Alpha particles ionise the air between electrodes; smoke absorbs them, reducing the current [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between contamination and irradiation, and state which is generally more dangerous and why.
practice_questions.marks: Irradiation: exposure to radiation from an external source; stops when source removed; person/object does not become radioactive [1 mark]. Contamination: radioactive material on or inside the body; continuous exposure even after leaving the original source [1 mark]. Contamination is generally more dangerous [1 mark] because the source remains close to cells and continues to irradiate them, with no way to remove the exposure [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why the moderator and the control rods in a nuclear reactor serve different functions.
practice_questions.marks: Moderator slows neutrons to speeds at which they are most effective at triggering fission in U-235 [1 mark]; without it, fast neutrons are less likely to cause fission [1 mark]. Control rods absorb neutrons to regulate the rate of the chain reaction [1 mark]; inserting them further reduces the reaction rate and withdrawing them increases it [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A patient is given a radioactive tracer for a PET scan. Explain why the tracer used must have a short half-life, and why it must be produced nearby.
practice_questions.marks: Short half-life: the tracer decays quickly after the scan, reducing the patient’s total radiation dose [1 mark]. Also, rapid decay means high initial activity, providing a detectable signal without requiring a large quantity of radioactive material [1 mark]. Produced nearby: because the half-life is short (e.g. approximately 110 minutes for fluorine-18), the tracer would decay significantly during transport [1 mark]; it must be used within hours of production, so a cyclotron must be located close to the scanning facility [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of nuclear fission as an energy source compared to burning fossil fuels.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8–9): balanced evaluation covers: advantages of fission (no CO2 during operation, high energy density, reliable baseload power, finite but long-lasting uranium supply) and disadvantages (radioactive waste, long storage periods, high construction and decommissioning costs, public perception and safety risk, low-probability but high-consequence accidents). Fossil fuel advantages (established infrastructure, dispatchable, relatively cheap) and disadvantages (CO2 contributing to climate change, air pollution, finite supply, price volatility). Justified conclusion that neither is ideal; the best choice depends on balancing climate targets against waste and safety concerns. Secure (5–7): develops both sides with specific points. Developing (3–4): lists points without evaluative comparison. Emerging (1–2): simple relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why nuclear fusion requires extremely high temperatures to occur, and describe the main challenge this creates for building a practical fusion reactor.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): explains that at low temperatures protons (nuclei) repel each other due to electrostatic repulsion between positive charges [1]; high temperature gives nuclei sufficient kinetic energy to overcome this repulsion and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to take over and cause fusion [1]; at these temperatures matter exists as a plasma that cannot be contained by physical materials [1]; must be confined by magnetic fields (e.g. in a tokamak) or laser compression [1]; achieving net energy gain (output > input) has not yet been demonstrated at power-plant scale [1]; the economic and engineering barriers make commercial fusion still distant [1]. Secure (3–4): explains repulsion and temperature requirement plus one containment point. Developing (2): explains the temperature requirement. Emerging (1): states that high temperature is needed.
